messages.subject: Error in rcpp_states_list_to_DEmat
parts:
Hi Nick (and all), 

I am a graduate student at San Diego State University and after reading your review of The Monkey's Voyage, I became very interested in BioGeoBEARS. I have successfully ran the example files and have modified your script to run some of my own data. My tree has 43 taxa, 17 areas, and a max area of 10 (as the extant species that has the largest range occurs in 10 areas). When I load my files in and check the inputs everything looks great and I get no error messages. However at the end of running the DEC analysis when I prompt R to produce PDF plots, I get the following error message and the PDF file that was created is corrupt and will not open. 

Error in rcpp_states_list_to_DEmat(areas_list, states_list, dmat, elist,  : 
  negative length vectors are not allowed

I have been researching this problem and have not found any solutions. I have also tried changing my initial parameters with no luck. I am hoping that someone will have an idea of why this error is occurring. 

Thank you very much for your time, 
Shannon

messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Re: Error in rcpp_states_list_to_DEmat
parts:
Hi Shannon,

So, the problem is the number of areas and your max range size.  You have 17 areas and the largest species occupies 10 of them.  That means that the state space (number of possible geographic ranges, ie number of combinations of presence/absence in each region that are possible) is:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=17, maxareas=max_range_size, include_null_range=TRUE)

109294

...which means a transition matrix of size 109294x109294. This matrix would have 11,945,178,436 cells. Even storing this in memory would be problematic, let alone doing the matrix exponentiation calculations which are done for the likelihood calculations.

So, R probably freaked out while trying to set up this matrix, or, if you left max_range_size as the default, 4, that would cause a different area when it tries to code a range of 10 areas into a state space where 4 areas is the maximum.


BACKGROUND:

(number of states) = (size of state space) = 2^(number of areas in analysis), or less if (max number of areas in a range) < (number of areas in analysis)

...and...

size of transition matrix = (number of states)^2

The maximum practical size of the transition matrix in BioGeoBEARS is something like 2000 states, ie a 2000x2000 rate matrix, perhaps a bit more with serious multicore supercomputing.

Yes, this is annoying and is a huge limit with the whole field.  The only current solution is the "BayArea" program, Landis et al. 2013, SysBio, but it doesn't do cladogenesis processes at the moment:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic


SHORTER VERSION: Please read the script starting from:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script
=======================================
# KEY HINT: The number of states (= number of different possible geographic ranges)
# depends on (a) the number of areas and (b) max_range_size.
=======================================


SOLUTIONS IN BIOGEOBEARS: Merge some areas, divide up the analysis, and/or force certain taxa to have narrower ranges, so that you can lower numareas and/or maxareas.  You need to get this:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=17, maxareas=10, include_null_range=TRUE)

...below 2000 if you want to have much hope of the run finishing, or below about 600 if you want it to run in < 1 day.

Cheers!
Nick

On Thursday, November 13, 2014 7:58:04 PM UTC-8, Nick Matzke wrote:
Hi Shannon,

So, the problem is the number of areas and your max range size.  You have 17 areas and the largest species occupies 10 of them.  That means that the state space (number of possible geographic ranges, ie number of combinations of presence/absence in each region that are possible) is:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=17, maxareas=max_range_size, include_null_range=TRUE)

109294

...which means a transition matrix of size 109294x109294. This matrix would have 11,945,178,436 cells. Even storing this in memory would be problematic, let alone doing the matrix exponentiation calculations which are done for the likelihood calculations.

So, R probably freaked out while trying to set up this matrix, or, if you left max_range_size as the default, 4, that would cause a different area when it tries to code a range of 10 areas into a state space where 4 areas is the maximum.


BACKGROUND:

(number of states) = (size of state space) = 2^(number of areas in analysis), or less if (max number of areas in a range) < (number of areas in analysis)

...and...

size of transition matrix = (number of states)^2

The maximum practical size of the transition matrix in BioGeoBEARS is something like 2000 states, ie a 2000x2000 rate matrix, perhaps a bit more with serious multicore supercomputing.

Yes, this is annoying and is a huge limit with the whole field.  The only current solution is the "BayArea" program, Landis et al. 2013, SysBio, but it doesn't do cladogenesis processes at the moment:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic


SHORTER VERSION: Please read the script starting from:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script
=======================================
# KEY HINT: The number of states (= number of different possible geographic ranges)
# depends on (a) the number of areas and (b) max_range_size.
=======================================


SOLUTIONS IN BIOGEOBEARS: Merge some areas, divide up the analysis, and/or force certain taxa to have narrower ranges, so that you can lower numareas and/or maxareas.  You need to get this:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=17, maxareas=10, include_null_range=TRUE)

...below 2000 if you want to have much hope of the run finishing, or below about 600 if you want it to run in < 1 day.

Cheers!
Nick
